chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-1.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.1)* A family has two children, at least one of which was born on a Tuesday. (Each child's day of birth is uniform over the 7 weekdays, independently, and the children are ordered by birth.) What is the probability that the first one was born on a Tuesday?

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-2.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.2)* Suppose you are being tested for a disease which everyone has a $1\%$ chance of having. If you have it, then the test will come up positive. If you don't, then the test will come up negative with $97\%$ chance and positive with $3\%$ chance. Given that the test came up positive, what is the probability that you actually have the disease?

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3a.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.3(a))* Events $A$ and $B$ are *independent* iff $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. Determine whether the following events are independent. If $x$ is the outcome of one die roll: $A=$ ($x$ is even) and $B=$ ($x$ is a multiple of $3$).

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3b.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.3(b))* Events $A$ and $B$ are *independent* iff $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. Determine whether the following events are independent. If $x$ is the outcome of one die roll: $A=$ ($x$ is a multiple of $3$) and $B=$ ($x$ is a multiple of $4$).

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3c.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.3(c))* Events $A$ and $B$ are *independent* iff $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. Determine whether the following events are independent. If $x$ is the outcome of one die roll: $A=$ ($x$ is odd) and $B=$ ($x$ is prime).

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3d.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.3(d))* Events $A$ and $B$ are *independent* iff $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. Determine whether the following events are independent. For a randomly chosen day: $A=$ (it is a Friday) and $B=$ (it is the 13th of a month). (Assume every month has $31$ days, so every $31$ days it becomes a new month.)

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3e.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.3(e))* Events $A$ and $B$ are *independent* iff $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. Determine whether the following events are independent. In a random permutation of $\{1,2,3\}$: $A=$ (the 1st number is greater than the 2nd) and $B=$ (the 2nd number is greater than the 3rd).

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-3f.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.3(f))* Events $A$ and $B$ are *independent* iff $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. Determine whether the following events are independent. In a sequence of coin flips: $A=$ (the substring HH first appears before the substring TT does) and $B=$ (the substring HT first appears before the substring TH does).

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-4.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.4)* Suppose $X$ is a random variable taking real values between $0$ and $1$ such that the likelihood of each outcome is proportional to its value. What is the appropriate probability density function $f$ from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb R$?

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-5.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.5)* An unfair coin, with $P(\text{head})=\frac1n$, is flipped repeatedly. What is the expected number of times it must be flipped until a head appears?

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-6.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.6)* Two random variables $X,Y$ are *independent* if $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)P(Y=y)$ (discrete) or $f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)$ (continuous). Prove that for independent $X,Y$ and every possible outcome $y$ of $Y$, $E[X]=E[X\mid Y=y]$. Treat the discrete case and the continuous case separately.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-6.answer: Proof: the conditional distribution of $X$ given $Y=y$ equals the distribution of $X$

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-7.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.7)* Prove that $E[X]\le\sqrt{E[X^2]}$ for (1) a discrete random variable $X$ and (2) a continuous random variable $X$. (Hint: use Hölder's inequality $\sum|a_ib_i|\le(\sum|a_i|^p)^{1/p}(\sum|b_i|^q)^{1/q}$, $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$, and its integral version.)

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-8.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.8)* For random variables $X,Y$ on the same probability space (not necessarily independent), prove the tower rule $E[X]=E\big[E[X\mid Y]\big]$ in the discrete case and in the continuous case. (Hint: Fubini's theorem.)
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-8.answer: Proof: write $E[X\mid Y=y]$ as a sum/integral and swap the order of summation

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-9.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.9)* Prove that for independent random variables $x,y$ with finite expectations, $E[xy]=E[x]E[y]$, in the discrete case and in the continuous case.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-9.answer: Proof: factor the joint probability mass/density function

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-10.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.10)* A *(discrete-time) martingale* is a sequence $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with $E|X_n|<\infty$ and $E[X_n\mid X_{n-1},\dots,X_1]=X_{n-1}$. Prove that $E[X_n]=E[X_1]$ for all positive integers $n$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-11.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.11)* A *(discrete-time) martingale* is a sequence $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with $E|X_n|<\infty$ and $E[X_n\mid X_{n-1},\dots,X_1]=X_{n-1}$. A *stopping function* $f$ takes finite sequences of numbers and outputs True/False. For a sample $(x_1,x_2,\dots)$ let $k$ be the least index with $f(x_1,\dots,x_k)=$ True, and assume $k$ exists with probability $1$. Define $X'_n=x_n$ if $f(x_1,\dots,x_j)$ is False for all $j\le n-1$, and $X'_n=X'_{n-1}$ otherwise (i.e. $X'_n=X_{\min(n,k)}$). Prove that $X'=(X'_1,X'_2,\dots)$ is a martingale.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-11.answer: Proof: on $\{k\le n-1\}$ the value is frozen; on $\{k\ge n\}$ it follows $X$

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-12.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.12)* A *(discrete-time) martingale* is a sequence $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with $E|X_n|<\infty$ and $E[X_n\mid X_{n-1},\dots,X_1]=X_{n-1}$. A *stopping function* $f$ takes finite sequences of numbers and outputs True/False. For a sample $(x_1,x_2,\dots)$ let $k$ be the least index with $f(x_1,\dots,x_k)=$ True, and assume $k$ exists with probability $1$. Define $X'_n=x_n$ if $f(x_1,\dots,x_j)$ is False for all $j\le n-1$, and $X'_n=X'_{n-1}$ otherwise (i.e. $X'_n=X_{\min(n,k)}$). Let $S=|x_1|+|x_2-x_1|+\dots+|x_k-x_{k-1}|$. Show that $|X'_n|\le S$ for every $n$.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-12.answer: Proof: telescoping and the triangle inequality

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-14.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.14)* A *(discrete-time) martingale* is a sequence $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with $E|X_n|<\infty$ and $E[X_n\mid X_{n-1},\dots,X_1]=X_{n-1}$. Find a counterexample: a martingale together with a stopping function for which $k$ exists with probability $1$ but $E[x_k]\ne E[x_1]$.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-14.answer: Simple random walk $X_n$ with $X_1=0$, $\pm1$ steps, stopped when it first hits $1$: $E[x_k]=1\ne0=E[x_1]$

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-15.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.15)* You are walking on a number line with endpoints $0$ and $100$, and you are currently at $67$. Every second, you flip a fair coin and walk one step forward if it is heads and one step backward if it is tails, until you reach either $100$ or $0$. What is the probability that you reach $100$ before $0$? (Hint: find a martingale.)

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-16.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.16)* In the same situation (fair coin, endpoints $0$ and $100$, start at $67$), what is the expected number of seconds it takes to reach one of the endpoints? Use a martingale (hint: optional stopping).

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-17.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.17)* You are walking on a number line between $0$ and $100$, currently at $67$, with an unfair coin: the chance of heads (one step forward) is $h$ and of tails (one step backward) is $1-h$, with $0<h<1$. What is the probability that you reach $100$ before $0$, in terms of $h$?

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-18.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.18)* You are walking on a number line between $0$ and $1$ and are currently at $0.6$, but the fairness of the coin depends on where you are: every second, if you are located at coordinate $x$ then with probability $x$ you get a head and move $0.05$ units forward, while with probability $1-x$ you get a tail and move $0.05$ units backward. What is the probability that you reach $1$ before $0$?

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-19.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.19)* The *variance* of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[(X-E[X])^2]=E[X^2]-E[X]^2$. Compute the variance of one fair die roll.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-20.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.20)* Compute the variance of a random real number sampled uniformly from the interval $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-21.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.21)* Prove that the variance of the sum of two independent random variables is the sum of their variances: $\mathrm{Var}(x+y)=\mathrm{Var}(x)+\mathrm{Var}(y)$. (Use $E[xy]=E[x]E[y]$ for independent variables.)

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-22.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.22)* Compute the variance of the sum of $n$ independent fair die rolls.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-23.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.23)* Prove that if every outcome of a random variable $X$ is multiplied by $\lambda$, the variance scales by $\lambda^2$: $\mathrm{Var}(\lambda X)=\lambda^2\mathrm{Var}(X)$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-24.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.24)* The *standard deviation* of a data set is the square root of its variance (the mean of squared deviations from the mean). How many standard deviations away from the mean are each of the five elements of the set $\{0,3,4,6,12\}$?
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-24.answer: Mean $5$, $\sigma=4$: the elements are $\frac54,\ \frac12,\ \frac14,\ \frac14,\ \frac74$ standard deviations away (for $0,3,4,6,12$ respectively)

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-25.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.25)* (Chebyshev's inequality) Show that for any data set of real numbers with standard deviation $\sigma>0$ and any positive integer $n$, at most a fraction $\frac1{n^2}$ of the data lies at least $n$ standard deviations away from the mean.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-26.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.26)* Use the previous problem to obtain a $75\%$ confidence interval for the sum of $1000$ die rolls: an interval which contains at least $75\%$ of the sums obtained when sets of $1000$ dice are rolled and summed.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-27.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.27)* You play a game in which you start with $\$1$ and flip a fair coin repeatedly. Every head increases your money by $25\%$; as soon as you get a tail you must stop. What is your expected final amount of money?

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-28.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.28)* In the previous game (start with $\$1$, flip a fair coin repeatedly, stop at the first tail), suppose instead every head increases your money by $100\%$. Creating the recursion as before gives $E=E+\frac12$, i.e. $0=\frac12$, which is clearly false. What happened?
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-28.answer: The expected final amount is infinite, so the equation cannot be manipulated like a finite number

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-29.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.29)* In the same game, suppose every head increases your money by $200\%$ (the amount triples). The recursion gives $E=\frac32E+\frac12$, hence $E=-1$, negative, but you can never lose money. What happened?
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-29.answer: The expected final amount is infinite, so the recursion is not valid

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-1-30.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.30)* A real number is randomly chosen between $0$ and $1$ and written in base $3$ as $0.xyz\ldots_3=\frac x3+\frac y9+\frac z{27}+\cdots$ (digits $x,y,z,\ldots\in\{0,1,2\}$). It is then interpreted as a decimal in base $9$: $0.xyz\ldots_9=\frac x9+\frac y{81}+\frac z{729}+\cdots$. What is the expected value of the square of this base-$9$ decimal? (Hint: use variance.)

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-1.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.1)* Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be independent random variables (not necessarily identically distributed) with $X_i\in[0,1]$, let $S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n$, $\mu_n=E[S_n]$, $t>0$ and $\lambda>0$. Show that $P(e^{\lambda S_n}\ge e^{\lambda(\mu_n+t)})\le e^{-\lambda(\mu_n+t)}\,E[e^{\lambda X_1}]E[e^{\lambda X_2}]\cdots E[e^{\lambda X_n}]$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-2.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.2)* Prove that $\dfrac{e^{\lambda x}-1}{\lambda x}\le\dfrac{e^\lambda-1}\lambda$ for all $x\in(0,1]$ and $\lambda>0$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-3.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.3)* Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be independent random variables (not necessarily identically distributed) with $X_i\in[0,1]$, let $S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n$, $\mu_n=E[S_n]$, $t>0$ and $\lambda>0$. Show that $\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n\big(1+E[X_i](e^\lambda-1)\big)\le\left(1+\frac{e^\lambda-1}n\mu_n\right)^n$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-4.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.4)* The $n$-th moment of a random variable $x$ is $E[x^n]$ (it *exists* if $E|x|^n<\infty$). Prove that if the $n$-th moment exists, then so do all lower moments (the $0$-th through $(n-1)$-th).

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-5.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.5)* Prove that the moments about a real number $b$ can be computed from the moments about $a$: $E[(x-b)^n]=\sum_{i=0}^n\binom niE[(x-a)^i](a-b)^{n-i}$ (assuming the moments exist).
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-5.answer: Proof: binomial theorem on $(x-b)=(x-a)+(a-b)$ and linearity

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-6.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.6)* Let $X$ be a sample from the normal distribution $N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)$ with density $\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}$ and $Y$ an independent sample from $N(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)$. Show that $X+Y$ has distribution $N(\mu_1+\mu_2,\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)$. (The density of $X+Y$ is the convolution $f(z)=\int f_X(x)f_Y(z-x)dx$.)
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-6.answer: Proof: complete the square in the convolution integral

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-7.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.7)* The moment generating function of a random variable $X$ is $M_X(t)=E[e^{tX}]$. Compute the moment generating function of the normal distribution $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ and show it equals $e^{t\mu+\sigma^2t^2/2}$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-8.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.8)* Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2>0$, and $Y_i=\frac{X_i-\mu}\sigma$. Show that each $Y_i$ has mean $0$ and variance $1$.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-8.answer: Proof: linearity of expectation and scaling of variance

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-9.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.9)* Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2>0$, and $Y_i=\frac{X_i-\mu}\sigma$. Assume all moments of $Y_i$ exist. Let $S_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Expanding $E[S_n^k]=n^{-k/2}\sum_{k_1+\dots+k_n=k}\binom k{k_1,\dots,k_n}E[Y_1^{k_1}\cdots Y_n^{k_n}]$, show: (a) the sum of the terms in which some $k_i=1$ is $0$; (b) the sum of the terms with no $k_i=1$ but some $k_i\ge3$ is at most $C_kn^{(k-1)/2}$ (so these terms contribute $O(n^{-1/2})$ to $E[S_n^k]$ and tend to $0$); (c) the terms in which every $k_i\in\{0,2\}$ sum to $0$ if $k$ is odd and tend to $(k-1)!!=(k-1)(k-3)\cdots3\cdot1$ if $k$ is even. Conclude that $E[S_n^k]\to(k-1)!!$ for even $k$ and $\to0$ for odd $k$.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-9.answer: Proof: independence factorizes each term; count the tuples

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-10.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.10)* Show that the moments of the standard normal distribution $N(0,1)$ are $E[G^k]=0$ for odd $k$ and $E[G^k]=(k-1)!!=(k-1)(k-3)\cdots3\cdot1$ for even $k$, and conclude that the limits of the moments of $S_n$ (from the previous problem: $0$ for odd $k$, $(k-1)!!$ for even $k$) are exactly the moments of $N(0,1)$.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-10.answer: Proof: odd moments vanish by symmetry; integrate by parts for the even ones

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-11.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.11)* Carleman's condition: if $\sum_{i=1}^\infty\mu_{2i}^{-1/(2i)}=\infty$, where $\mu_{2i}$ are the even moments of a distribution, then the moments determine the distribution uniquely (up to equivalence of cumulative distribution functions). Prove that a probability distribution having the same moments as $N(0,1)$ is equivalent to $N(0,1)$.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-11.answer: Proof: Carleman's condition holds for the moments $(2i-1)!!$

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-12.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.12)* Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2>0$, and $Y_i=\frac{X_i-\mu}\sigma$. Let $S_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Show that the moment generating function of $S_n$ is $M_{S_n}(t)=\big(E[e^{tY_1/\sqrt n}]\big)^n$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-13.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.13)* Let $e^x=1+x+\frac{x^2}2+R(x)$. Use the Lagrange error bound to bound $R(x)$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-14.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.14)* Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2>0$, and $Y_i=\frac{X_i-\mu}\sigma$. Assume $E[e^{s|Y_1|}|Y_1|^3]<\infty$ for all $s$ (e.g. the moment generating function exists). Show that $E[e^{tY_1/\sqrt n}]=1+\frac{t^2}{2n}+R(t,Y_1,n)$ where $|R(t,Y_1,n)|$ is bounded by $\frac C{n^{3/2}}$ with $C$ not depending on $n$.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-14.answer: Proof: expand $e^{x}$ with $x=tY_1/\sqrt n$ and bound the remainder

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-15.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.15)* Let $|R_n|\le Cn^{-3/2}$. Show that $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{t^2}{2n}+R_n\right)^n=e^{t^2/2}$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-16.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.16)* Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. with $E[X]=0$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=1$ and $E|X|^3\le Q$; let $S_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$, let $G_1,G_2,\dots$ be independent $N(0,1)$ samples independent of the $X_i$, and let $f$ be a function with three bounded derivatives, $|f'''|\le C$. Let $T_{n-1}=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}X_i$. Use the Lagrange error bound to show $E[f(S_n)]=E\Big[f\Big(T_{n-1}+\frac{X_n}{\sqrt n}\Big)\Big]=E[f(T_{n-1})]+\frac{E[f''(T_{n-1})]}{2n}+\mathrm{Error}$ with $|\mathrm{Error}|\le\frac{E|X_n|^3}{6n^{3/2}}C$.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-16.answer: Proof: Taylor expansion to second order, independence and $E[X]=0$, $E[X^2]=1$

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-17.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.17)* Let $G\sim N(0,1)$. Compute $E|G|^3$ and show it equals $\sqrt{8/\pi}$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-18.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.18)* Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. with $E[X]=0$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=1$ and $E|X|^3\le Q$; let $S_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$, let $G_1,G_2,\dots$ be independent $N(0,1)$ samples independent of the $X_i$, and let $f$ be a function with three bounded derivatives, $|f'''|\le C$. Assume (as in the previous problems) that for the normal sample $E\big[f(T_{n-1}+\frac{G_n}{\sqrt n})\big]=E[f(T_{n-1})]+\frac{E[f''(T_{n-1})]}{2n}+\mathrm{Error}'$ with $|\mathrm{Error}'|\le\frac{E|G|^3}{6n^{3/2}}C$. Show that $\Big|E[f(S_n)]-E\Big[f\Big(\frac{G_1}{\sqrt n}+\dots+\frac{G_n}{\sqrt n}\Big)\Big]\Big|\le n\cdot\frac{E|X|^3+\sqrt{8/\pi}}{6n^{3/2}}C$.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-18.answer: Proof: replace the variables one at a time (hybrid argument) and add the errors

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-19.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.19)* Let $G_1,\dots,G_n$ be independent $N(0,1)$ samples. Show that $\frac{G_1}{\sqrt n}+\dots+\frac{G_n}{\sqrt n}$ has distribution $N(0,1)$.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-19.answer: Proof: scaling and the sum of independent normals

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-20a.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.20(a))* For reals $r$ and $\epsilon>0$ define $f_{r,\epsilon}(x)=0$ for $x\le r-\epsilon$; $f_{r,\epsilon}(x)=\dfrac{\int_{-1}^{(x-r)/\epsilon}(t+1)^3(t-1)^3dt}{\int_{-1}^{1}(t+1)^3(t-1)^3dt}$ for $r-\epsilon\le x\le r+\epsilon$; and $f_{r,\epsilon}(x)=1$ for $x\ge r+\epsilon$. Show that $f_{r,\epsilon}$ is thrice differentiable (its first, second and third derivatives exist).

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-20b.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.20(b))* For reals $r$ and $\epsilon>0$ define $f_{r,\epsilon}(x)=0$ for $x\le r-\epsilon$; $f_{r,\epsilon}(x)=\dfrac{\int_{-1}^{(x-r)/\epsilon}(t+1)^3(t-1)^3dt}{\int_{-1}^{1}(t+1)^3(t-1)^3dt}$ for $r-\epsilon\le x\le r+\epsilon$; and $f_{r,\epsilon}(x)=1$ for $x\ge r+\epsilon$. Show that the absolute value of the third derivative of $f_{r,\epsilon}$ is bounded by $\dfrac{105}{16\epsilon^3}$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-21.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.21)* For reals $r$ and $\epsilon>0$ define $f_{r,\epsilon}(x)=0$ for $x\le r-\epsilon$; $f_{r,\epsilon}(x)=\dfrac{\int_{-1}^{(x-r)/\epsilon}(t+1)^3(t-1)^3dt}{\int_{-1}^{1}(t+1)^3(t-1)^3dt}$ for $r-\epsilon\le x\le r+\epsilon$; and $f_{r,\epsilon}(x)=1$ for $x\ge r+\epsilon$. Let $\mathrm{Ind}_p(x)=1$ if $x\ge p$ and $0$ otherwise. Show that for any random variable $W$ (in particular $S_n$ or a normal sample $G$): $E[\mathrm{Ind}_p(W)]\in\big[E[f_{p+\epsilon,\epsilon}(W)],\,E[f_{p-\epsilon,\epsilon}(W)]\big]$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-22a.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.22(a))* For reals $r$ and $\epsilon>0$ define $f_{r,\epsilon}(x)=0$ for $x\le r-\epsilon$; $f_{r,\epsilon}(x)=\dfrac{\int_{-1}^{(x-r)/\epsilon}(t+1)^3(t-1)^3dt}{\int_{-1}^{1}(t+1)^3(t-1)^3dt}$ for $r-\epsilon\le x\le r+\epsilon$; and $f_{r,\epsilon}(x)=1$ for $x\ge r+\epsilon$. Let $G\sim N(0,1)$. Prove $\big[E f_{p+\epsilon,\epsilon}(G),E f_{p-\epsilon,\epsilon}(G)\big]\subseteq\big[E\,\mathrm{Ind}_{p+2\epsilon}(G),E\,\mathrm{Ind}_{p-2\epsilon}(G)\big]$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-22b.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.22(b))* Let $G\sim N(0,1)$ and $\epsilon>0$. Show that $E[\mathrm{Ind}_{p-2\epsilon}(G)]-E[\mathrm{Ind}_{p+2\epsilon}(G)]\le\frac{4\epsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-23.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.23)* From the previous results, for every $p$ and every $\epsilon>0$, $\big|E[\mathrm{Ind}_p(S_n)]-E[\mathrm{Ind}_p(G)]\big|\le\dfrac{4\epsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}+\dfrac{E|X|^3+\sqrt{8/\pi}}{6\sqrt n}\cdot\dfrac{105}{16\epsilon^3}$. Find a constant $K$, depending only on the distribution of $X$ (through $E|X|^3$) and not on $n$, such that the right-hand side is always at least $K\,n^{-1/8}$ (and equals it for the best $\epsilon$).

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-24.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.24)* The Weak Law of Large Numbers: for i.i.d. $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2>0$, and $\bar X_n=\frac{X_1+\dots+X_n}n$, for every $\varepsilon>0$, $\lim_{n\to\infty}P(|\bar X_n-\mu|<\varepsilon)=1$. Prove it using the Central Limit Theorem (the standardized sample mean $\frac{\sqrt n}\sigma(\bar X_n-\mu)$ converges in distribution to $N(0,1)$).
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-2-24.answer: Proof: $P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)=P(|Z_n|\ge\varepsilon\sqrt n/\sigma)\le P(|Z_n|\ge M)\to P(|G|\ge M)$ for every fixed $M$

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-1.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.1)* (Infinite monkey theorem) Let $S$ be a set and $X_0,X_1,\dots$ independent identically distributed random variables with values in $S$ such that $P(X_0=s)>0$ for all $s\in S$. Prove that for every finite sequence $s_0,s_1,\dots,s_k$ of elements of $S$, $P(\exists n:\ X_n=s_0,X_{n+1}=s_1,\dots,X_{n+k}=s_k)=1$. (Borel–Cantelli: if $\sum P(A_n)=\infty$ and the $A_n$ are independent then infinitely many $A_n$ occur with probability $1$.)
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-1.answer: Proof: the events on disjoint blocks of length $k+1$ are independent, each of probability $q>0$; apply Borel–Cantelli II

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-2.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.2)* Prove that there exists a *simply normal number*: a real number $x\in[0,1]$ such that for every integer base $d>1$ and every $a\in\{0,\dots,d-1\}$ the digit $a$ occurs in the base-$d$ representation of $x$ with asymptotic frequency $\frac1d$: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\#\{\text{occurrences of }a\text{ among the first }n\text{ digits}\}}n=\frac1d$. (Use the first Borel–Cantelli lemma: if $\sum P(A_n)<\infty$ then with probability $1$ only finitely many $A_n$ occur.)
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-2.answer: Proof: for a uniform random $x$, the digits are i.i.d. uniform; a fourth-moment bound plus Borel–Cantelli I gives almost sure convergence; take a countable intersection over $(d,a)$

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-3.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.3)* Find a sequence of independent random variables $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with $P(X_n\in\{-n,n,0\})=1$ and $E[X_n]=0$ for each $n$, such that the weak Law of Large Numbers holds but not the strong one: for $Y_n=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$, for every $\varepsilon>0$ we have $P(|Y_n|\ge\varepsilon)\to0$, but $P(\lim_nY_n=0)\ne1$.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-4.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.4)* A Markov chain $X_0,X_1,\dots$ on a finite or countable state space $S$ satisfies $P(X_n=x_n\mid X_0=x_0,\dots,X_{n-1}=x_{n-1})=P(X_n=x_n\mid X_{n-1}=x_{n-1})$; it is time homogeneous if $P(X_n=y\mid X_{n-1}=x)=P(x,y)$ does not depend on $n$, and $P$ is its transition matrix. Prove that for all $m,n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$, $P(X_{m+n}=y\mid X_n=x)=P^m(x,y)$, where $P^m$ is the $m$-th matrix power.

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-5.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.5)* A Markov chain $X_0,X_1,\dots$ on a finite or countable state space $S$ satisfies $P(X_n=x_n\mid X_0=x_0,\dots,X_{n-1}=x_{n-1})=P(X_n=x_n\mid X_{n-1}=x_{n-1})$; it is time homogeneous if $P(X_n=y\mid X_{n-1}=x)=P(x,y)$ does not depend on $n$, and $P$ is its transition matrix. The chain is *irreducible* if for every ordered pair $(x,y)$ there is $m>0$ with $P^m(x,y)>0$. Its associated graph has a directed edge $x\to y$ whenever $P(x,y)>0$. Prove that the chain is irreducible iff the associated graph is strongly connected (there is a directed path from every vertex to every other vertex). (Reversing all edges does not affect strong connectedness, so the orientation convention is immaterial.)
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-5.answer: Proof: $P^m(x,y)>0$ iff there is a path of length $m$ from $x$ to $y$

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-6.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.6)* A Markov chain $X_0,X_1,\dots$ on a finite or countable state space $S$ satisfies $P(X_n=x_n\mid X_0=x_0,\dots,X_{n-1}=x_{n-1})=P(X_n=x_n\mid X_{n-1}=x_{n-1})$; it is time homogeneous if $P(X_n=y\mid X_{n-1}=x)=P(x,y)$ does not depend on $n$, and $P$ is its transition matrix. Let the chain be irreducible with $P(X_0=x_0)=1$, and let $T_x=\min\{n>0:X_n=x\}$. It is *recurrent* if $P(T_{x_0}<\infty)=1$. Prove that the following are equivalent: (2) for some $x$, $P(X_n=x\text{ infinitely often})=1$; (3) for all $x$, $P(X_n=x\text{ i.o.})=1$; (4) for some $x$, $\sum_mP^m(x,x)=\infty$; (5) for all $x$, $\sum_mP^m(x,x)=\infty$.
chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-6.answer: Proof: $P_x(N_x\ge j+1)=\rho_x^j$ gives $\rho_x=1\iff\sum P^m(x,x)=\infty\iff P_x(\text{i.o.})=1$; irreducibility transfers this between states

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-7.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.7)* A Markov chain $X_0,X_1,\dots$ on a finite or countable state space $S$ satisfies $P(X_n=x_n\mid X_0=x_0,\dots,X_{n-1}=x_{n-1})=P(X_n=x_n\mid X_{n-1}=x_{n-1})$; it is time homogeneous if $P(X_n=y\mid X_{n-1}=x)=P(x,y)$ does not depend on $n$, and $P$ is its transition matrix. chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-7.answer: Proof: the chain resets to $1$ infinitely often and each time has probability $2^{-2025}$ to go straight up to $2026$

chmmc-cmm-2026-power-3-8.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.8)* The *independent random walk on $\mathbb Z^d$* is the Markov chain with $P(x,y)=2^{-d}$ if $|x_i-y_i|=1$ for every $i\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ and $0$ otherwise (in each coordinate it performs an independent simple $\pm1$ random walk).
